cw-everyday-norms:
The Typo That Changed a Team

Host: Picture a newer colleague three months into the job. They send a client letter with one typo. Within an hour it comes up in a team chat, in a reply-all and in a one-on-one. Nobody is unkind. So what did that colleague just learn?

Co-host: That a typo is a big deal here. Probably bigger than the policy says. And that the safest move is to have three people check every routine letter from now on.

Host: Right. Nobody wrote that rule down. The team taught it in an afternoon. That is what culture is: the shared habits and assumptions that tell people what really matters, mostly without words.

Co-host: But accuracy matters. A wrong address on a notice can mean someone misses an appointment. I don't want us to get casual about that.

Host: Neither do I. The question isn't whether to keep a high standard. It's whether the response matches the stakes. A clear check for things that can hurt someone is a standard. Treating every small slip as a crisis is a habit, and it has costs.

Co-host: Like the three reviewers for a routine letter. That's time those reviewers aren't spending with families.

Host: And something quieter. When mistakes feel dangerous, people stop mentioning them. Research on team learning has found that stronger teams sometimes report more errors, not fewer, because people feel safe enough to say so.

Co-host: So the number of mistakes you hear about isn't the same as the number that happen.

Host: Exactly. Silence can look like quality from the outside.

Co-host: Say a notice did go out with the wrong office address, and a client traveled to the old location. What does a good response sound like?

Host: Start with the person affected: fix it for them first. Then ask what about the process let it happen, before asking who. Was the address stored in three places? Did the template pull an old value?

Co-host: And the person who sent it is in the room, probably feeling awful.

Host: Which is why the supervisor goes first if they can. Something like, here's what happened, here's what we've already fixed for the client, and here's the part of our process I want us to look at together.

Co-host: Here's the harder one for me. What if the mistake is the supervisor's? A wrong deadline in the team update, and you're the newest person there.

Host: Keep it short, private and about the work. I think the report deadline in the update might be the 15th, not the 20th. Want me to check? That's it. No apology tour.

Co-host: And if the supervisor thanks them for it, in front of the team, the next person speaks up faster.

Host: That's how a norm shifts. Not with a poster. With what happens the next time someone says, I think we got this wrong.

Co-host: In the course, you'll practice telling standards from habits, and responding to mistakes in a way that keeps people talking.
cw-sustainable-pace:
Running on Empty, Quietly

Host: Here's someone a lot of us know. A case manager, two years with a full caseload, and really good at it. Lately they answer email at ten at night, skip lunch and feel flat even after a good outcome for a family.

Co-host: Nothing's on fire. The work is getting done. So is there actually a problem?

Host: That's the trap. The early signs are quiet. Feeling flat after a win is one of them. The World Health Organization describes burnout as a result of workplace stress that hasn't been managed: exhaustion, growing distance from the work and feeling less effective.

Co-host: So it's about the conditions at work, not a personal failing.

Host: Right. And that matters, because it means some of the fixes are things a team can change together.

Co-host: Okay, practical moment. It's 9:45 at night. A colleague emails a non-urgent question about next week's schedule. I'm going to answer it. It takes thirty seconds.

Host: It does. And it also tells your colleague that late-night answers are normal here. Next week, they'll feel they should answer at ten, too.

Co-host: Huh. So the thirty seconds isn't really the cost.

Host: No. One small protection is to schedule the reply for the morning, or simply answer it at nine. The question still gets answered. The norm doesn't spread.

Co-host: What about when it's more than email? Caseload up by a third since spring, two reports late, and I haven't said anything to my supervisor.

Host: That's the moment to raise it, while it's two reports and not ten. Bring facts and a question: here's what's changed, here's what's slipping, which of these should I put first?

Co-host: That's much easier to say than, I'm not coping.

Host: And it's more useful to a supervisor. They can actually decide something.

Co-host: Last one. A colleague has seemed withdrawn for a few weeks and left early twice without saying goodbye. I don't want to pry.

Host: You don't have to diagnose anything. A private, simple check-in works: I've noticed you seem a bit quieter lately. How are you doing? Then listen, and let them decide how much to share.

Co-host: And if they're really struggling?

Host: Know where support lives. Minnesota's state Employee Assistance Program is free, voluntary and confidential, for state employees and the people they live with. And if someone may be in crisis, the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline answers by call, text or chat, any time.

Co-host: So the course isn't about fixing anyone. It's about noticing early, and knowing the next step.
cw-pace-pressure-decisions:
Is It Really Due Today?

Co-host: Four in the afternoon. A supervisor gets a request: send updated guidance to every case manager by end of day. The guidance changes how a form is filled out, and the supervisor hasn't read it closely.

Host: First question: who set the end of day, and what happens if it goes out tomorrow morning instead?

Co-host: Sometimes the answer is, a law says so. Often it's, someone just said by end of day.

Host: And that difference matters. Research on decisions under time pressure finds people shift to shortcuts. They look at less information and lean on what's quick. Fine for low stakes. Risky for guidance a whole division will follow.

Host: Here's another. The monthly report shows four hundred cases closed, a record. The program manager is preparing remarks.

Co-host: Celebrate it, surely. People worked hard.

Host: Celebrate the effort, yes. But ask what four hundred closures means for people. How many closed because services started, and how many because a form wasn't returned?

Co-host: Ah. A closed case isn't the same as a family that got help.

Host: Output is what we produce. Outcomes are what changes for people. Under pressure, output is easier to count, so it quietly becomes the goal.

Co-host: So what do you actually do in the moment? End of day, a case manager is about to close a case because a form never came back.

Host: A short pause routine. Three questions: who does this affect, what would I need to know to be confident, and is anything about this situation unusual?

Co-host: And in this case a colleague mentions the household's preferred language isn't English, and the reminder went out in English only.

Host: Then the pause just did its job. The right next step is a reminder they can read, not a closure.

Co-host: But some deadlines can't move. A new eligibility process launches on a date set by law, and notices in Somali and Hmong won't be ready for two more weeks.

Host: Then you protect quality another way. A quick premortem helps: imagine it's a month after launch and it went badly for families who read Somali or Hmong. What happened?

Co-host: They never heard about the change. Or they heard and didn't know what to do.

Host: So you plan for that now: community partners, interpreters on the phone line, extra time to respond. The date holds. The harm doesn't have to.

Co-host: That's the whole course: tell a true deadline from a habit, and protect the decisions that matter most.
cw-workload-burnout:
The Person Who Always Says Yes

Co-host: A team lost two positions last year, and the work stayed the same. Two people are on leave. Then a difficult new case comes in, the kind one case manager always handles well.

Host: And that case manager is already covering more than anyone. So it goes to them. Again.

Co-host: It's efficient, though.

Host: Today. The burnout research points to six areas of work life that matter: workload, control, reward, community, fairness and values. Giving the hard case to the same person every time touches at least three of them.

Co-host: So the supervisor raises it in a one-on-one, and the case manager says, I'm fine, it's just a busy season.

Host: But the supervisor has seen late-night emails for most of the month. The mistake would be to argue about whether they're fine.

Co-host: Because they'll just dig in.

Host: Right. Name what you've noticed, without judgment, and make it about the work. I've seen a lot of late emails this month. That tells me the load isn't working. What's one thing I could take off or move?

Co-host: So the supervisor owns the problem, instead of asking the person to admit they're struggling.

Host: Exactly. Workload is a design problem. The supervisor has the levers.

Co-host: Here's where I get nervous. A supervisor proposes a shared weekly view of caseloads. As a newer person, I'd worry it'll be used to judge whoever is slower.

Host: That worry is the whole design question. Say clearly what the view is for: spotting when one person is overloaded and moving work. Not ranking anyone. Agree it as a team, and review it after a month.

Co-host: And notice who doesn't speak. If someone with years on the team stays silent, that's worth a private follow-up.

Host: Last piece. The program manager asks the supervisor how the team is doing. Caseloads up thirty percent, two people on leave, two reports late.

Co-host: The instinct is to say, we're managing.

Host: And then nothing changes above you. Give the facts plainly, say what's at risk, and bring a choice: here's what we can keep on time, here's what will slip, which would you protect?

Co-host: That's not complaining. That's giving your manager something to decide.

Host: And it protects your team. That's what this course practices: seeing the drivers, holding the conversation, and changing how the work is shared.
cw-learning-organization:
When Leaders Hear "Resistance"

Host: Three months after a new intake process launched, a manager in the leadership meeting says frontline staff are resisting it. Two other supervisors say the same thing.

Co-host: As a director, I'd hear that as a change management problem. More training, more communication.

Host: Maybe. But resistance is often information arriving in a form leaders don't like. What are staff seeing that we aren't? The research on learning organizations says culture is built by systems: how we gather information, how we review, how we decide.

Co-host: Then a case manager asks for five minutes and says the new form is causing families to give up partway through. And I championed that form.

Host: That's the moment that decides whether the next person comes to you. What's your first sentence?

Co-host: Honestly? Probably a defense of why we built it.

Host: Most of us would. Try, thank you for bringing this to me directly. Show me where families stop. Then the follow-up matters even more: tell them what you did with it.

Co-host: Because the whole floor will know how that conversation went by lunch.

Host: Now a blameless review of a missed deadline. Partway through, a supervisor starts to say which case manager made the error.

Co-host: And the facilitator has to step in.

Host: Kindly and quickly. Something like, let's stay with how the process worked, and come back to individual follow-up separately. The point of the review is to find what the system made easy to get wrong.

Co-host: Which is why the facilitator shouldn't be the person whose decision is under review.

Host: Last one. The program manager has a draft policy ready. It changes how families submit paperwork. The county partner and the counties haven't seen it.

Co-host: Sending it as final saves weeks.

Host: It might. But the people closest to families will find the problems eventually. The only question is whether they find them before launch or after. Share it as a draft, say what can still change, and set a date.

Co-host: So a learning organization isn't a slogan. It's a set of routines leaders design and protect.

Host: That's what this course is for: building those routines in your own division.
cw-trauma-informed-teams:
A Lobby Like a Police Station

Co-host: A county partner tells a program manager that families describe the lobby as like a police station. The security check is required, and several families have left before their interviews.

Host: So the check stays. The question is everything around it. SAMHSA's trauma-informed approach has six principles: safety, trustworthiness and transparency, peer support, collaboration, empowerment and choice, and attention to cultural, historical and gender issues.

Co-host: Run the lobby through those, and you get practical ideas. A sign that explains why the check exists. A greeting before the screening, not after. A place to wait that doesn't feel like a holding area.

Host: None of that weakens security. It just stops security from being the first and only message.

Host: Here's the appointment letter a case manager is asked to revise. You must appear at the office on the date below. Failure to appear will result in case closure.

Co-host: Accurate. And frightening, if you've had bad experiences with systems.

Host: Keep the facts and change the stance. Lead with what the appointment is for, offer a way to reschedule and say who to call. The consequence can still be there, stated plainly, near the end.

Co-host: Now the staff side. A team handled a child fatality review this week. Several people were closely involved. The program manager wants to respond.

Host: Secondary traumatic stress is real. The National Child Traumatic Stress Network describes it as the emotional duress that results when a person hears about the firsthand trauma experiences of another.

Co-host: So a cheerful team lunch isn't the answer.

Host: Not on its own. Acknowledge what happened, offer some flexibility with the next few days, and remind people about the Employee Assistance Program, which is confidential. Then check in again next week, not just once.

Co-host: Last one is mine to lead. A leadership meeting will cover a staff assault from last month. Some people in the room were there when it happened.

Host: Tell people beforehand what will be discussed, so nobody is surprised. Say at the start that stepping out is fine. Keep the focus on what the division is changing, not on reliving the details.

Co-host: Choice and transparency again.

Host: Exactly. The six principles work for staff as much as for families. That's the heart of this course.
